title: When Federal Express Staff Were Asked to Hold Their Pay Cheques
dek: A year after its first night in 1973, Fred Smith's courier airline was losing money fast, and he kept it flying on conviction, new capital and, by his account, one night in Las Vegas.

story.event: Keeping the new air courier alive through its first years of losses
story.summary: Federal Express began full overnight operations from Memphis on 17 April 1973 with 14 small jets and 186 packages. Rising fuel costs and slow early volume left it losing heavily; staff were sometimes asked not to cash their pay cheques, and by Fred Smith's own account he won $27,000 at blackjack in Las Vegas after General Dynamics turned down a request for capital. He raised more money, the company ran at a loss for 26 months, and it made its first profit in 1976.
paragraphs: On the night of 17 April 1973, fourteen Dassault Falcon 20 jets flew out of Memphis on the first full night of Federal Express. By the company's count they carried 186 packages to 25 American cities; fifty years later Fred Smith remembered 189, and said every one arrived overnight. It was a small load for a network built at full size from the first day, planes and trucks feeding one sorting hub, because Smith believed the system could not work any smaller.

The money ran short almost at once. Smith had put in $4 million he had inherited and, by the end of 1972, raised about $80 million in loans and equity; other accounts put the total nearer $90 million. Then fuel prices climbed, costs outran revenue, and by mid-1974, Entrepreneur later reported, the company was losing more than $1 million a month. "We'd run out of money," Smith said in 1998. More than once he asked employees not to cash their pay cheques; Audrey Phifer, hired in the first year, remembered holding hers "a couple of times". His half-sisters, he said, were upset because it looked as if they would lose money.

The best-known moment of that year rests on Smith's own telling. After General Dynamics turned down his request for capital, he was flying home from Chicago when, on impulse, he went to Las Vegas instead, played blackjack and won $27,000, which he wired back to the company. "The $27,000 wasn't decisive, but it was an omen that things would get better," he said. What carried him, he said in 1998, was conviction and loyalty to the people who had signed on with him. "I wasn't afraid to lose my money," he said, and "if we were going to go down, we were going to go down with a fight."

He raised another $11 million after Las Vegas and kept the planes flying. Federal Express ran at a loss for 26 months before it broke even. Accounts of the losses differ: nearly $13.4 million in the first two years (Entrepreneur, 2008), $27 million in two years (the Academy of Achievement) or $29 million in three (CBS News, 2023). In 1976 it made its first profit, $3.6 million, and in 1978 it went public.

quote.text: Let the property of thy friend be as dear to thee as thine own
quote.source_title: Pirke Avot: The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, tr. Joseph I. Gorfinkle, Project Gutenberg eBook #8547
quote.connection: Smith said he was not afraid to lose his own money. Rabbi Jose asks for something harder: to hold a friend's property as dear as one's own. Smith's staff were holding their wages and his family's money was at risk, and the night in Las Vegas was a bet placed while theirs was on the line.

reflection: Smith's nerve was real, and so was the patience of the people around him. Employees who held their pay cheques were lending him something they could not easily spare, and none of them had a say in the trip to Las Vegas.

When you are tired and sure you are right, it is easy to count only your own stake. Anything worth building soon tangles other people's resources with yours: a colleague's evenings, a family's patience, someone's savings. It helps to know plainly whose reserves a hard month is really drawing on, and to tell them where things stand.
invitation: Name one person whose time or money is quietly tied up in what you are building. Today, tell them one honest thing about how it is going, good or bad.

sources.title: Frederick W. Smith: interview and biography
sources.supports: Smith's own words on the 1974 crisis: 'We'd run out of money'; half-sisters upset at the prospect of losing money; 'I wasn't afraid to lose my money'; loyalty to those who had signed on; 'if we were going to go down, we were going to go down with a fight'. Biography text: 14 jets and 186 packages on the first night; 25 cities; $80 million raised (a caption says $91 million); $27 million lost in the first two years.

sources.title: Fred Smith: An Overnight Success
sources.supports: 14 Falcon jets, 25 cities and 186 packages on the first night; $80 million in loans and equity by the end of 1972; $4 million of Smith's inheritance; rising fuel prices; losses of more than $1 million a month by mid-1974 and nearly $13.4 million in the first two years; General Dynamics turning him down; the flight home from Chicago and the impulsive trip to Las Vegas; $27,000 won at blackjack; Smith's 'The $27,000 wasn't decisive, but it was an omen that things would get better'; another $11 million raised; a $3.6 million profit in 1976; public two years later.

sources.title: FedEx: A 50-year revolution of business
sources.supports: Smith recalling '189 pieces' on the first night, all delivered overnight; $29 million lost in the first three years; Smith asking employees not to cash their paychecks; Audrey Phifer's recollection that 'it happened a couple of times that we had to hold our checks'.

sources.title: Who Made America? Frederick W. Smith
sources.supports: The network had to be built whole rather than started small; the 25-city network went live on 17 April 1973; about $90 million in venture capital; twenty-six months at a loss before breaking even.

sources.title: FedEx Celebrates 50 Years of Operations
sources.supports: First overnight operations from Memphis on 17 April 1973 with 14 Dassault Falcon 20s delivering 186 packages to 25 US cities, according to the airline; the hub concept.

sources.title: How Fred Smith rescued FedEx from bankruptcy by playing blackjack in Las Vegas
sources.supports: Fuel costs and investors' refusal to put in more; General Dynamics' board declining; the stop in Las Vegas and $27,000 won at blackjack and wired back, as reported by Forbes; another $11 million raised afterwards.

sources.title: FedEx Corp.
sources.publisher: Gale Encyclopedia of E-Commerce, via Encyclopedia.com
sources.supports: $91 million in venture capital and $4 million inherited; 14 Falcons in 1973; struggling to meet expenses including payroll; General Dynamics rejecting a loan request; $27,000 won at blackjack in Las Vegas; first profit in 1976; IPO in April 1978.

sources.title: FedEx founder Fred Smith has died
sources.supports: Incorporated in 1971 and flying from 1973; early losses; blackjack winnings in Las Vegas keeping the company running while Smith sought more capital.

cross_checks.claim: Full operations began on 17 April 1973 with 14 Falcon jets carrying 186 packages to 25 cities (Smith later recalled 189).
Smith raised roughly $80-91 million before and around launch, plus $4 million of his own inheritance.
The company ran out of money and staff were asked to hold their pay cheques.
After General Dynamics turned him down, Smith won $27,000 at blackjack in Las Vegas (his own telling).
Federal Express lost money for its first years (26 months at a loss) and made its first profit in 1976.

research_notes: Loss figures disagree and the story gives all three with who said what: nearly $13.4 million in the first two years (Entrepreneur, 2008), $27 million in the first two years (Academy of Achievement biography) and $29 million in the first three years (CBS News, 2023); PBS says 26 months at a loss, which the story also uses. Capital raised: $80 million in loans and equity by the end of 1972 (Entrepreneur; Academy of Achievement text), about $90 million (PBS) and $91 million (Academy of Achievement caption; Gale); the story gives about $80 million and 'nearer $90 million'. First night: 186 packages in every written source, but Smith told CBS in 2023 'I think we had 189 pieces'; both are given. Entrepreneur's 2008 article wrongly dates the start of operations to April 1971 (the year of incorporation); 17 April 1973 is confirmed by PBS and Airways. The 1976 figure of $3.6 million is profit in Entrepreneur but 'sales' in the Gale encyclopedia entry; profit is used, since Fox Business puts 1976 revenue at about $75 million. Las Vegas: the story rests on Smith's own telling; written sources narrate it (Entrepreneur, Fox Business citing Forbes, Gale, the Daily Memphian) and Entrepreneur quotes Smith calling it an omen rather than decisive. Accounts differ on the stake (often given as the company's last $5,000) and on what the money paid for (fuel or payroll), so the story gives neither; one popular retelling gives $32,000 rather than $27,000 and is not cited. The 1974-75 criminal case over a forged loan-guarantee document, in which Smith was acquitted, is not covered by any source that loaded, so it is left out. The Achievement interview is dated 23 May 1998, with the interviewer placing the crisis 24 years earlier, in 1974. Rabbi Jose's saying is applied by analogy.
